questions.prompt: (Textbook 6.1, HW6) Can both `insert` and `findMin` be implemented in **constant** time for a priority queue? Explain how, say what you give up, and compare with a binary heap.
questions.answer:
**Yes.** Keep the elements in an unsorted list (or vector) together with one extra variable `minSoFar`. `insert(x)` appends x (O(1)) and updates `minSoFar = min(minSoFar, x)` (one comparison, O(1)); `findMin` returns `minSoFar` (O(1)).

What you give up is `deleteMin`: after removing the minimum we no longer know the new minimum without scanning all the remaining elements, so `deleteMin` is O(N) (a priority queue needs insert **and** deleteMin to be fast).

A binary heap: `findMin` is O(1) **worst case** (it is the root), but `insert` is O(1) only **on average** (O(log N) worst case, when the new element is a new minimum and percolates up to the root), and `deleteMin` is O(log N). So the heap gives up a little on insert to get a fast deleteMin.
rubric: Says yes and describes a concrete structure (unsorted list/array plus a stored minimum)
insert updates the minimum with one comparison: O(1); findMin returns it: O(1)
Identifies the cost: deleteMin becomes O(N) (needs a rescan)
Compares with a heap: findMin O(1) worst, insert O(1) average / O(log N) worst, deleteMin O(log N)

questions.prompt: (Textbook 6.4, HW6) A complete binary tree with N elements uses array positions 1..N (children of i at 2i and 2i+1). Suppose we use the same array representation for a binary tree that is **not** complete. How large must the array be (as a function of N) for: (a) a tree with two extra levels (its deepest node is two levels deeper than in a complete tree), (b) a tree whose deepest node is at depth 2 log N, (c) a tree whose deepest node is at depth 4.1 log N, (d) the worst-case tree? Logs are base 2.
questions.answer:
A node at depth d has an index of at most 2^(d+1) - 1, so the array must reach index 2^(d+1) - 1 where d is the depth of the deepest node. A complete tree of N nodes has d = floor(log N) and needs N cells.

(a) d = floor(log N) + 2: highest index < 2^(floor(log N) + 3) <= **8N** cells (a constant-factor blow-up, O(N)).
(b) d = 2 log N: 2^(2 log N + 1) = 2 x 2^(2 log N) = **2N^2** cells.
(c) d = 4.1 log N: 2^(4.1 log N + 1) = **2 N^4.1** cells.
(d) The worst case is a "stick" (every node has exactly one child), depth N - 1: 2^N - 1 cells, **exponential**. So an array only works when the tree is complete (or nearly).
rubric: Uses 'deepest node at depth d needs index up to 2^(d+1) - 1' as the principle
(a) about 8N (constant factor)
(b) 2N^2 and (c) 2N^4.1 (powers of N)
(d) 2^N - 1, exponential for a chain
Grows the array when full and increments currentSize to create the hole

questions.prompt: (Textbook 6.7a, HW6) Prove that for binary heaps, `buildHeap` does at most 2N - 2 comparisons between elements. (You may use the fact that a tree is a complete binary tree with nodes at known heights; give a self-contained argument for the sum of the heights.)
questions.answer:
**Cost of one percolateDown.** Each iteration of the loop in `percolateDown` makes **2** element comparisons (smaller child vs. smaller child; smaller child vs. the moved value) and moves the hole down **one level**. The hole can move at most `height(i)` levels, so `percolateDown(i)` makes **at most 2 height(i)** comparisons.
Total comparisons <= 2 H, where H = the sum of the heights of all the nodes.

**Lemma: H(N) = N - b(N) <= N - 1** (b(N) = number of 1 bits of N, always >= 1).
Proof: delete all the leaves of the complete tree. The remaining nodes are exactly the internal nodes, positions 1..floor(N/2), and they form a complete tree. Every internal node's height in the old tree is exactly **1 more** than in the new tree (an internal node whose children were all leaves had height 1 and now has height 0; any other internal node has height 1 + the height of its taller *internal* child, and that child's height dropped by 1 by induction from the bottom), and the leaves had height 0. Hence H(N) = H(floor(N/2)) + floor(N/2), H(1) = 0. Unrolling: H(N) = floor(N/2) + floor(N/4) + floor(N/8) + ... < N/2 + N/4 + ... = N (this is exactly the slides' series N/2 + N/4 + ...). The closed form N - b(N): if N = 2m then b(N) = b(m) and 2m - b(m) = N - b(N); if N = 2m+1 then b(N) = b(m) + 1 and 2m - b(m) = N - b(N). Since b(N) >= 1, H <= N - 1.

**Conclusion:** comparisons <= 2H <= 2(N - 1) = **2N - 2**. (For N = 15: H = 11, so at most 22 comparisons; the book's Figure 6.15 example uses 10 percolation steps = 20 comparisons.)
rubric: Counts 2 comparisons per level of percolateDown and at most height(i) levels for node i
Reduces the total to 2 x (sum of heights of all nodes)
Proves (or correctly cites with justification) sum of heights <= N - 1 (N - b(N), or the series N/2 + N/4 + ...)
Concludes 2(N - 1) = 2N - 2

questions.prompt: (Textbook 6.8, HW6) Show the following about the **maximum** item in a binary min-heap with N elements: (a) it must be at one of the leaves; (b) there are exactly N/2 leaves (give the exact count for odd and even N); (c) every leaf must be examined to find it.
questions.answer:
(a) Suppose a maximum item is at an internal node v. v has a child c, and heap order gives key(c) >= key(v), so c holds a maximum too (keys are at most the maximum). Repeat from c; the walk ends at a node with no children, i.e. a leaf. So **some leaf holds a maximum** (if keys are distinct, the maximum is at a leaf).
(b) Node i has a child iff 2i <= N, so the internal nodes are exactly 1..floor(N/2) and the leaves are floor(N/2)+1..N: **N - floor(N/2) = ceil(N/2)** leaves ("N/2" for even N; (N+1)/2 for odd N).
(c) Suppose some leaf L is never examined by an algorithm that claims to find the maximum. Take the actual heap and replace L's key by a value bigger than every other key. L has no children and only needs to be >= its parent, so the result is still a valid heap with an identical answer to every comparison the algorithm made, yet now L holds the unique maximum. So the algorithm cannot be correct unless it looks at **all ceil(N/2) leaves**: finding the max of a heap is Theta(N), and the heap order gives almost no help (half the elements are leaves).
rubric: (a) Argument that a max cannot be strictly inside: a child is >= its parent, so push the maximum down to a leaf
(b) Internal nodes are 1..floor(N/2) (2i <= N), leaves = ceil(N/2)
(c) Adversary/replacement argument: an unexamined leaf can be made the maximum while the heap stays valid
Concludes finding the max is Theta(N), not O(1) or O(log N)

questions.prompt: (Textbook 6.10b and 6.10c, HW6) (b) Does the O(K) "find all nodes less than X" algorithm extend to other heap structures (leftist heaps, skew heaps, binomial queues)? (c) Describe an algorithm that finds an **arbitrary** item X in a binary min-heap (of N elements) using at most about 3N/4 element comparisons, and justify the count. (A plain linear scan uses N.)
questions.answer:
**(b)** Yes. The algorithm only uses heap order (a parent is <= its descendants) on a tree, not the array layout, so it works on leftist and skew heaps unchanged (root-to-children traversal with pruning), and on a binomial queue by running it on each of the (at most log N) binomial trees, O(K + log N).

**(c)** Facts: about N/2 nodes are leaves, about N/4 are the parents of leaves (height 1), about N/4 have height >= 2.
1. For each node p of height 1 (parent of leaves) compare X with p. If **X < p**: neither leaf child (>= p > X) can be X: skip them (cost 1). If X = p: found. If **X > p**: compare X with p's (at most 2) leaf children: cost <= 3. So this phase costs **at most 3 per height-1 node, <= 3 x N/4 = 3N/4** comparisons.
2. If p < X, every ancestor a of p satisfies a <= p < X, so a cannot be X: **no comparison needed** for any ancestor of such a p.
3. A remaining node of height >= 2 is one all of whose height-1 descendants had p > X (so each of them cost only 1 comparison instead of 3, a saving of 2 each); compare X with it directly (1 comparison). There are fewer such nodes than height-1 nodes below them, so the saving pays for them, and the total stays about 3N/4.
If X is found anywhere along the way, stop. (A leaf, height-1 node, or higher node holding X is always reached: a higher node holding X would have no descendant smaller than it, so it is never skipped.)
rubric: (b) Yes: only the heap-order property is used; works for any heap-ordered tree (binomial queue: once per tree, extra O(log N))
(c) Uses the fact that about half the nodes are leaves and a quarter are their parents
Compares with the parent of leaves first; if X < parent, skips both leaves
Uses that ancestors of a smaller node need no comparison, and counts about 3N/4 in the worst case

questions.prompt:
(Textbook 6.18a-d, HW6) A **min-max heap** supports both `deleteMin` and `deleteMax` in O(log N). Its structure is that of a binary heap (complete tree, array layout). Heap order: a node X at **even** depth is smaller than its parent but larger than its grandparent (where these exist), and a node X at **odd** depth is larger than its parent but smaller than its grandparent. (So even levels are "min levels" and odd levels are "max levels"; every node on a min level is the minimum of its subtree, every node on a max level is the maximum of its subtree.)
(a) How do you find the minimum and the maximum? (b) Give an algorithm to insert a new element. (c) Give algorithms for deleteMin and deleteMax. (d) Can you build a min-max heap in linear time?
questions.answer:
**(a)** The minimum is the **root** (depth 0, a min level). The maximum is the **larger of the root's two children** (the depth-1 nodes are the tops of the max levels; if N = 1 it is the root). Both O(1).

**(b) insert x:** place x at the next leaf position; let q be its parent. If x is on a **min** level and x > q (q is on a max level, so q should be >= x): swap x and q, then percolate x up along the **max** levels (compare with the grandparent; while x > grandparent, swap). Otherwise percolate x up along the **min** levels (while x < grandparent, swap with it). If x is on a max level the roles are reversed (if x < q swap, then bubble up along min levels; else bubble up along max levels). Each step goes up two levels: O(log N).

**(c) deleteMin:** remove the root; move the last element x to the root; **trickle down**: let m be the smallest among the children and grandchildren of the current node i. If m is a grandchild and m < x: swap x and m; if x (now at m's position, a min level) is larger than its new parent (a max level), swap those two as well; continue trickling from m's position. If m is a child and m < x: swap and stop. Otherwise (m >= x) stop. **deleteMax** is symmetric, starting from the root's larger child (the maximum), moving the last element there, and trickling down using the largest among children and grandchildren. Each is O(log N).

**(d) Yes, in O(N):** run the trickle-down from i = N/2 down to 1 (the min version if i's depth is even, the max version if odd). Each call costs O(height(i)), and the sum of the heights is O(N) (Theorem 6.1), exactly as for ordinary buildHeap.
rubric: (a) Min at the root; max is the larger root child; O(1)
(b) Insert at the end, then fix with a parent comparison and percolation up along same-type levels (grandparent chain); O(log N)
(c) deleteMin: last element to the root and trickle down choosing among children and grandchildren (with the extra parent swap); deleteMax symmetric
(d) Yes: trickle down from N/2 to 1; O(N) by the sum-of-heights argument

questions.prompt:
(HW6 Question 4, with Question 3 restated) Question 3 asked you to implement LeetCode's "Kth Largest Element in a Stream": a class constructed with an integer `k` and a vector `nums`, with `int add(int val)` that appends `val` to the stream and returns the k-th largest element so far. The suggested solution keeps a min-heap `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>` containing the k largest values: `add` pushes `val` and pops if the size exceeds k.
How could you make this solution more efficient if you manipulated the underlying vector directly instead of using the `priority_queue` methods? Give the new complexities.
questions.answer:
Baseline: the constructor does n pushes: O(n log k) (the heap never exceeds k+1 elements); every `add` does a push and a pop: two O(log k) operations, O(log k) total.

Improvements by working on a `vector<int> heap` with `<algorithm>` heap functions (or hand-written percolate routines), keeping a min-heap of the k largest (`greater<int>`):
1. **Build the initial heap in linear time.** Choose the k largest of `nums` (e.g. `nth_element` with `greater<int>` in O(n)), keep them in the vector, and call `make_heap(heap.begin(), heap.end(), greater<int>())`: **O(n)** (buildHeap on k items is O(k)), versus O(n log k) for n pushes.
2. **Skip work for small values.** If the heap already has k items and `val <= heap.front()` (the current k-th largest), `val` can never matter: return `heap.front()` immediately, **O(1)**, with no heap change (the priority_queue version still did a push and a pop).
3. **Replace the root instead of pop + push.** If `val > heap.front()`, overwrite the root with `val` (`heap[0] = val`) and percolate it **down** once (one O(log k) operation, about half the comparisons/moves of a deleteMin + insert). The library way (`pop_heap` then `heap.back() = val` then `push_heap`) is still two O(log k) steps; a hand-written `percolateDown` on the vector does it in one. `priority_queue` cannot replace its top in place.

Complexities: construction O(n) (instead of O(n log k)); `add` O(1) when val is not among the k largest and O(log k) otherwise with a smaller constant; `add` is still O(log k) worst case, but no longer pays for a separate push.
rubric: States the baseline cost: n pushes O(n log k) and push+pop O(log k) per add
Builds the initial heap with make_heap/buildHeap in O(n)
Skips the heap update when val <= current k-th largest (O(1))
Replaces the root and percolates down once instead of pop + push
States the resulting complexities

(b) **Always true**: all ancestors of a node are smaller than it, and only one key (the minimum, at the root) is smaller than the second smallest, so its only ancestor is the root: it is a child of the root (index 2 or 3).

(e) **Impossible**: an internal node in a perfect tree has two children, both larger than it, so at least two keys are larger than any internal key. The second-largest has only one key above it, so it is a leaf.
(f) **Always true**: the k-th smallest key has all its ancestors smaller, so its depth is at most k - 1: the 3rd smallest is at depth <= 2 (depth 2 is possible, depth 3 would need 3 smaller ancestors).

questions.prompt: Prove Theorem 6.1: for a perfect binary tree of height h (2^(h+1) - 1 nodes), the sum of the heights of all nodes is 2^(h+1) - 1 - (h + 1). Then use it to conclude that `buildHeap` is O(N).
questions.answer:
A perfect tree of height h has 2^i nodes at depth i, whose height is h - i. So
S = sum_{i=0..h} 2^i (h - i) = h + 2(h-1) + 4(h-2) + ... + 2^(h-1)(1).
Multiply by 2: 2S = 2h + 4(h-1) + 8(h-2) + ... + 2^h (1).
Subtract the first from the second: the terms almost cancel (2h - 2(h-1) = 2, 4(h-1) - 4(h-2) = 4, and so on); the last term of 2S, 2^h, has no partner in S, and the first term of S, h, has no partner in 2S, so 2S - S = -h + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... + 2^(h-1) + 2^h.
So S = (2 + 4 + ... + 2^h) - h = (2^(h+1) - 2) - h = **2^(h+1) - 1 - (h + 1)**.
With N = 2^(h+1) - 1 this is S = N - (h + 1) = N - log2(N + 1) < N.

**buildHeap:** `percolateDown(i)` moves a value down at most height(i) levels, each level costing O(1) (two comparisons), so the total is at most O(sum of heights). A complete tree of height h is a subtree of the perfect tree of height h (same shape, some bottom nodes missing) and every node's height is no larger, so its sum of heights is at most S < 2^(h+1) <= 2N (because N >= 2^h): O(N). (The book: exactly N - b(N).) Hence **buildHeap is O(N)**, not O(N log N).
rubric: Counts 2^i nodes at height h - i
Sets up S and 2S and subtracts correctly (or equivalent derivation)
Obtains S = 2^(h+1) - 1 - (h+1)

(b) Worst: keys in **decreasing** order into a min-heap: every new key is the new minimum and rises to the root: the i-th insert costs floor(log2 i) levels, total sum floor(log2 i) = Theta(N log N). Best: **increasing** order: each new key is >= its parent, no rise: O(1) each, O(N) total (even in the worst case for that input).
(c) "N/2 calls x O(log N)" is a valid upper bound but not tight: a call at a node of height h costs O(h), not O(log N), and most nodes are near the bottom (N/4 have height 1, N/8 height 2, ...). The sum of heights is N/4 + 2N/8 + 3N/16 + ... = O(N).

questions.prompt: (a) Why is a binary heap normally stored in an array rather than with nodes and pointers? (b) The array gives O(1) access by position. Why is that not considered a useful heap operation? (c) Why is index 0 left empty in the textbook implementation?
questions.answer:
(a) Because a heap is a **complete** binary tree, it fits in an array with no gaps: parent of i is i/2, children are 2i and 2i+1, so no links are needed. Benefits (slides): fewer memory allocations, better cache efficiency, and **O(1)** to add the new element at the end (the placement step of insert); navigation is just arithmetic. The drawback: you need a capacity estimate (resize by doubling).
(b) The k-th element of the array is **not** the k-th highest priority (the heap is only partially ordered), and position does not indicate order of insertion either. So reading by position tells you nothing useful; only the root (the highest priority) matters. Finding an arbitrary item still needs a scan, O(N).
(c) Index 0 is unused so that the child/parent arithmetic is `2i`, `2i+1`, `i/2`, with the root at 1. The textbook uses cell 0 as scratch space: the sentinel copy in `insert` that ends the percolate-up loop, and (in the HW6 trace convention) the value being moved. Other implementations start at 0 with children 2i+1 and 2i+2 (heapsort's layout).
rubric: (a) Complete tree => array with index arithmetic, no links; cache/allocation benefits; O(1) add at the end
(b) k-th array element is not the k-th priority; position is not insertion order
(c) Index 0 left empty for the 2i / 2i+1 / i/2 arithmetic and used as scratch (sentinel/tmp)

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a **priority queue** and a **binary heap**. Name two other ways to implement a priority queue and give their `insert` and `deleteMin` costs. What operation is a heap poor at, even though some graph algorithms need it?
questions.answer:
A **priority queue** is an abstract data type: a collection of elements with priorities that supports `insert` and removal of the highest-priority element (`deleteMin`), nothing about how it is stored. A **binary heap** is a *data structure* (a complete binary tree in an array with heap order) that implements it, just as a list ADT can be a linked list or an array.
Other implementations: an **unsorted list/vector** (insert O(1), deleteMin O(N)); a **sorted list/array** (insert O(N), deleteMin O(1)); a **balanced BST** such as an AVL tree (both O(log N) worst case, but more constant overhead and more features than needed); heap: insert O(log N) worst / O(1) average, deleteMin O(log N).
A heap is poor at **changing the priority of an element** (and finding any element, and merging): there is no efficient way to find where an element is without a scan, so decreaseKey/increaseKey/remove need the position to be known.

questions.prompt: You have N = 1,000,000 integers in memory and need the k-th largest. For each of the cases (i) k = 10, (ii) k = N/2 (the median), compare the textbook's algorithm 6A (buildHeap, then k deleteMins on a heap of all N elements) and algorithm 6B (maintain a heap of the k largest seen) in time and extra space, say which you would pick, and mention what quickselect adds. questions.answer:
**6A** (for the k-th *largest* use a max-heap): buildHeap O(N) + k deleteMax x O(log N) each = **O(N + k log N)**; extra space O(1) if the heap is built in place in the array.
**6B**: build a **min**-heap on the first k elements, O(k); for each of the remaining N - k elements compare with the root (the smallest of the k kept, O(1)); if larger, deleteMin + insert, O(log k). Total O(k + (N - k) log k) = **O(N log k)**; extra space O(k); works on a stream.

(i) k = 10: 6A is O(N + 10 log N) = O(N); 6B is O(N log 10) = O(N): both linear; 6B uses only 10 cells of extra memory and a single pass, so it is the better pick (also when the data is streamed).
(ii) k = N/2: 6A = O(N + (N/2) log N) = Theta(N log N); 6B = O((N/2) log(N/2)) = Theta(N log N); both Theta(N log N) (and 6B needs N/2 extra space). **Quickselect** (Ch 7) finds the k-th element in O(N) **average** (O(N^2) worst case), which beats both for the median.
Observation: when k = O(N / log N) algorithm 6A is O(N) (the buildHeap dominates); for k = N it is heapsort (O(N log N)).

questions.prompt: State the average-case cost of heap `insert` and give the two-part argument from lecture. Then give two situations where the argument does **not** apply, and the cost of `deleteMin` in the average case.
questions.answer:
`insert` is **O(log N) worst case but O(1) on average**. Insert has two steps: (1) put a placeholder for the new element at the end of the array, **O(1)**; (2) percolate up, which in the worst case takes log N steps (a new minimum reaches the root) but moves the element up **a constant number of levels on average**: the new element lands at the bottom level where half the nodes are, and for it to rise j levels it must beat the minimum of a subtree of about 2^(j+1) elements, whose probability falls geometrically (about 2^-(j+1)), so the expected rise is a convergent sum (the book: about 1.6 levels, 2.6 comparisons). This needs the inserted values to come from **the same distribution** as the values already in the heap. Hence N random inserts cost O(N) on average.
It does **not** apply (i) when keys arrive in **decreasing order** for a min-heap (each one rises to the root: Theta(log N) each) and (ii) when insertions and deleteMins are **alternated**: deleteMin removes the smallest elements, so the remaining ones are larger than a fresh element on average, and new elements rise far.
`deleteMin` is O(log N) in the worst case **and** on average: the element moved to the root came from the bottom, so it usually sinks almost all the way back.
rubric: States O(log N) worst, O(1) average
Two parts: O(1) placement at the end + constant expected percolate-up for same-distribution values
Names two failing situations (decreasing input; alternating insert/deleteMin)
deleteMin is O(log N) average too, with the reason

questions.prompt: Explain at a high level how a priority queue is used to simulate a bank with k tellers (textbook 6.4.2). What are the events, what is the key of the priority queue, why is it better than advancing a clock tick by tick, and what is the running time for C customers?
questions.answer:
The two **events** are a customer *arriving* and a customer *departing* (freeing a teller). Pending departures are kept in a **priority queue ordered by event time** (smallest time first); waiting customers are in an ordinary FIFO queue. The simulation repeatedly takes the next event: the earlier of the next arrival in the input and the smallest departure time in the heap, and advances the simulated clock **directly to that time**. An arrival takes a free teller (compute the departure time and insert it) or joins the line; a departure records statistics and, if somebody is waiting, starts the next customer (insert a new departure).
Ticking the clock one unit at a time would cost time proportional to the number of ticks (not part of the input size: multiply all times by 1,000 and it takes 1,000 times longer); jumping to the next event costs time proportional to the number of events.
With C customers there are 2C events, and the heap holds at most about k + 1 events, so each event costs O(log(k + 1)): total **O(C log(k + 1))**.
rubric: Events: arrival and departure; PQ keyed by event time (min = soonest)
Clock jumps to the next event instead of ticking
Arrival/departure processing described (teller free, queue of waiting customers)
Running time O(C log(k+1)) with reason (2C events, heap size about k+1)
Min-heap of at most k entries: value plus which list/position
Loop: pop the smallest, output it, push the successor from the same list
Correct STL declaration of a min-heap (greater<>) and handles empty lists
Analysis: N iterations x O(log k) = O(N log k), plus O(k log k) setup; space O(k) + output

questions.prompt: Insert 47 and then 22 into the **max**-heap `50,40,45,30,35,20,25,10,15` (textbook layout, index 1 first). Show index 0 (it holds the value being moved) and the hole `_` after each step. Give the final heap.
questions.answer:
For a max-heap every comparison is reversed: slide a parent down while the new key is **strictly larger** than it.

```
[0]=47 | 50 40 45 30 35 20 25 10 15 _        # insert 47: hole created at index 10; 47 stored in index 0
[0]=47 | 50 40 45 30 _ 20 25 10 15 35        # 47 > parent 35 (index 5) -> slide 35 down to index 10; hole moves to 5
[0]=47 | 50 _ 45 30 40 20 25 10 15 35        # 47 > parent 40 (index 2) -> slide 40 down to index 5; hole moves to 2
[0]=- | 50 47 45 30 40 20 25 10 15 35        # place 47 in index 2 (parent 50 is not smaller)
[0]=22 | 50 47 45 30 40 20 25 10 15 35 _     # insert 22: hole created at index 11; 22 stored in index 0
[0]=- | 50 47 45 30 40 20 25 10 15 35 22     # place 22 in index 11 (parent 40 is not smaller)
```

**Final heap:** `50,47,45,30,40,20,25,10,15,35,22`.
rubric: Reverses the comparison: a new key rises while it is larger than its parent
47 rises past 35 and 40 and stops below 50
22 stays at the bottom (its parent 40 is larger)

questions.prompt: Perform two `deleteMax` operations on the max-heap `90,70,80,40,60,50,75,10,30,20` (index 1 first). Show index 0 (it holds the value being moved) and the hole `_` after each step. State the removed elements and the final heap.
questions.answer:
Removed: **90, then 80**. The last element moves to the root and percolates down; the **larger** child moves up.

```
[0]=20 | _ 70 80 40 60 50 75 10 30           # deleteMax: remove 90 from the root (hole at 1); last element 20 goes to index 0; size 9
[0]=20 | 80 70 _ 40 60 50 75 10 30           # larger child 80 (index 3) beats 20 -> slide it up to index 1; hole moves to 3
[0]=20 | 80 70 75 40 60 50 _ 10 30           # larger child 75 (index 7) beats 20 -> slide it up to index 3; hole moves to 7
[0]=- | 80 70 75 40 60 50 20 10 30           # place 20 in index 7
[0]=30 | _ 70 75 40 60 50 20 10              # deleteMax: remove 80 from the root (hole at 1); last element 30 goes to index 0; size 8
[0]=30 | 75 70 _ 40 60 50 20 10              # larger child 75 (index 3) beats 30 -> slide it up to index 1; hole moves to 3
[0]=30 | 75 70 50 40 60 _ 20 10              # larger child 50 (index 6) beats 30 -> slide it up to index 3; hole moves to 6
[0]=- | 75 70 50 40 60 30 20 10              # place 30 in index 6
```

**Final heap:** `75,70,50,40,60,30,20,10`.
rubric: Last element moved to index 0 / the root hole
Larger child slides up; stops when the larger child is not bigger than the moved value

questions.prompt: Prove that a complete binary tree with N nodes has height floor(log2 N), so every heap operation that follows one root-to-leaf path is O(log N). Also prove that the parent of index i is i/2 (integer division) in the array layout.
questions.answer:
A complete tree of height h has all depths 0..h-1 full, and depth h has between 1 and 2^h nodes. So N >= (2^h - 1) + 1 = 2^h and N <= (2^h - 1) + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1 < 2^(h+1). Hence 2^h <= N < 2^(h+1), i.e. **h <= log2 N < h + 1**, so **h = floor(log2 N)** = O(log N). A root-to-leaf path has h + 1 nodes, so percolate up/down do at most h steps.

Layout: depth D occupies indices 2^D .. 2^(D+1) - 1 (induction: depth 0 has index 1; depth D+1 has twice as many nodes as depth D, and consecutive nodes of depth D at indices i, i+1, ... have their children at 2i, 2i+1, 2i+2, 2i+3, ... which are consecutive indices of depth D+1 starting at 2 x 2^D = 2^(D+1)). So node i has left child 2i and right child 2i+1; conversely, a node j is the child of floor(j/2) because j = 2i or 2i + 1 gives floor(j/2) = i.
rubric: Bounds N between 2^h and 2^(h+1) - 1 for height h
Concludes h = floor(log2 N) = O(log N)
Explains the index layout by level (2^D..2^(D+1)-1) or children 2i/2i+1
Derives parent = floor(j/2) from j = 2i or 2i+1
